How rapidly does a random fixed permutation mix pairs?

A uniformly sampled permutation on nn bits, fixed for the whole walk, takes exactly three cipher rounds to bring every starting pair within total variation 1/41/4 of uniform with probability tending to one as nn grows. At two cipher rounds the distance tends to e−1/2≈0.60653e^{-1/2}\approx0.60653. The third round averages over enough intermediate differences to make the distance vanish. The finite experiments below show how early this asymptotic behavior appears.

The fixed-threshold result and its finite bounds below are project derivations. The expected fraction of zero entries in a random XOR table is published, and earlier typical-ergodicity arguments make an additional graph-distribution assumption. A priority claim for the three-round theorem would require a further literature check. The final section gives a separate consequence of Liu, Tessaro and Vaikuntanathan's inverse calculation and classical trace counts.

Model and round count

Write N=2nN=2^n, m=N−1m=N-1, V=𝔽2nV=\mathbb F_2^n, and take n≥2n\ge 2. A cipher round applies x↦P(x+k)x\mapsto P(x+k), with a fresh uniform common key kk each round. Choose PP uniformly once when studying a random table. The following probabilities over keys are evaluated after fixing PP. For nonzero a,b∈Va,b\in V define

Tab=N−1#{x:P(x)+P(x+a)=b},Uab=1/m,M=T−U,dj=maxa12∑b|(Tj)ab−1/m|. T_{ab}=N^{-1}\#\{x:P(x)+P(x+a)=b\},\quad U_{ab}=1/m,\quad M=T-U,\quad d_j=\max_a \tfrac12\sum_b |(T^j)_{ab}-1/m|.

TT is doubly stochastic. Conditioned on a difference, the final random XOR makes the ordered pair uniform in its fiber of size NN. Those fibers are disjoint and the last permutation preserves distance to uniform. Thus the worst-start ordered-pair distance at cipher round r≥1r\ge1 is dr−1d_{r-1}. In particular the one-round distance is exactly d0=1−1/md_0=1-1/m.

The three-round theorem

For every fixed K>0K>0, with probability 1−OK(N−K)1-O_K(N^{-K}) over the uniform table,

d2=OK(logNN). d_2=O_K\!\left(\sqrt{\frac{\log N}{N}}\right).

Every row's one-step TV tends to e−1/2e^{-1/2} simultaneously in probability. Hence for fixed 0<ϵ<e−1/20<\epsilon<e^{-1/2} the worst-start pair mixing time is exactly three cipher rounds with probability tending to one. For e−1/2<ϵ<1e^{-1/2}<\epsilon<1 it is exactly two with probability tending to one. The argument leaves the behavior at the boundary ϵ=e−1/2\epsilon=e^{-1/2} open. Irreducibility and aperiodicity both hold except on an event of probability exp(−Ω(N))\exp(-\Omega(N)).

The matching behind a row

The unordered pairs {x,x+a}\{x,x+a\} for a fixed aa form a perfect matching on NN points. The image of this matching under uniform PP is a uniform perfect matching. Write Kab=NTab/2K_{ab}=NT_{ab}/2 for its number of shared edges with the fixed bb-matching. Every cell has the same marginal law. For the falling factorial (x)j=x(x−1)⋯(x−j+1)(x)_j=x(x-1)\cdots(x-j+1) and j≤N/2j\le N/2,

𝔼(Kab)j=(N/2)j(N−1)(N−3)⋯(N−2j+1). \mathbb E(K_{ab})_j = \frac{(N/2)_j}{(N-1)(N-3)\cdots(N-2j+1)}.

Indeed each ordered list of jj distinct edges of the bb-matching occurs in the image matching with probability the reciprocal of the displayed denominator. Each factor in the ratio is at most one and tends to 1/21/2 for fixed jj. For j>N/2j>N/2 the factorial moment vanishes. Inclusion-exclusion for Pr(Kab=0)\Pr(K_{ab}=0) and domination by ∑j1/j!\sum_j1/j! give Pr(Kab=0)→e−1/2\Pr(K_{ab}=0)\to e^{-1/2}.

Every positive cell of TT is at least 2/N>1/m2/N>1/m. Hence the exact one-step TV of a row is its number of missing differences divided by mm. Its mean is Pr(Kab=0)\Pr(K_{ab}=0), the same for every aa. The expected density of zero cells was determined by O'Connor. O'Connor, On the Distribution of Characteristics in Bijective Mappings

Transposing two images of PP changes at most two unordered edges in any input matching. Each changed edge moves mass 2/N2/N within its row. Consequently every row changes by at most 4/N4/N in TV or 8/N8/N in ℓ1\ell^1. The same bound holds for columns because T(P−1)=T(P)⊤T(P^{-1})=T(P)^\top.

If a real function of a uniform permutation changes by at most cc under such transpositions, revealing its images one at a time gives a martingale with increments bounded by cc. Two possible choices of the next image can be coupled by interchanging those two outputs in the completion. Azuma's inequality gives Pr(|f−𝔼f|>t)≤2exp[−t2/(2Nc2)]\Pr(|f-\mathbb Ef|>t)\le 2\exp[-t^2/(2Nc^2)]. Applying this with c=4/Nc=4/N and taking a union bound over the mm rows proves the simultaneous one-step claim.

Two-step energy for one table used twice

Directly from the first two factorial moments,

𝔼∑bTab2=3N−8N(N−3),𝔼∥M∥F2=𝔼∥T∥F2−1=2(N−2)2N(N−3). \mathbb E\sum_b T_{ab}^2=\frac{3N-8}{N(N-3)},\qquad \mathbb E\|M\|_F^2 =\mathbb E\|T\|_F^2-1=\frac{2(N-2)^2}{N(N-3)}.

The fourth moment 𝔼Kab4\mathbb E K_{ab}^4 is at most 1515 by expanding into falling factorials with coefficients 1,7,6,11,7,6,1 in increasing order. Cauchy–Schwarz across the m2m^2 cells gives 𝔼∥M∥F4≤𝔼∥T∥F4≤16(m/N)4𝔼Kab4≤240\mathbb E\|M\|_F^4\le \mathbb E\|T\|_F^4\le 16(m/N)^4\mathbb E K_{ab}^4\le 240. These calculations require only the marginal law of each cell.

Let LL be an independent uniform invertible linear map on VV and CC its permutation matrix on the mm nonzero differences, oriented so that T(LP)=T(P)CT(LP)=T(P)C. Any ordered pair of distinct nonzero vectors is linearly independent over 𝔽2\mathbb F_2. Therefore the linear group acts transitively on those ordered pairs. For any fixed MM, the average of CMM⊤C⊤CMM^\top C^\top has a constant diagonal and a constant off-diagonal. It kills the all-ones vector, and its trace is ∥M∥F2\|M\|_F^2. Thus

𝔼C[CMM⊤C⊤]=∥M∥F2m−1(I−U). \mathbb E_C[CMM^\top C^\top]=\frac{\|M\|_F^2}{m-1}(I-U).

LPLP is uniformly distributed, so we may calculate the energy of its square and average first over LL. Orthogonality of CC and M(I−U)=MM(I-U)=M give

𝔼P∥M2∥F2=𝔼P,C∥MCMC∥F2=𝔼P,Ctr(MCMM⊤C⊤M⊤)=𝔼P∥M∥F4m−1. \mathbb E_P\|M^2\|_F^2 =\mathbb E_{P,C}\|MCMC\|_F^2 =\mathbb E_{P,C}\operatorname{tr}(MCMM^\top C^\top M^\top) =\frac{\mathbb E_P\|M\|_F^4}{m-1}.

This averaging preserves the reuse of the same permutation in both factors. Conjugating PP by LL permutes both row and column indices together. By transitivity every row of M2M^2 therefore has the same expected squared Euclidean norm. Applying Cauchy–Schwarz to a row and Jensen's inequality to its mean gives

𝔼TV(eaT2,u)≤12𝔼∥M2∥F2≤60/(N−2), \mathbb E\,\mathrm{TV}(e_aT^2,u) \le \tfrac12\sqrt{\mathbb E\|M^2\|_F^2} \le \sqrt{60/(N-2)},

where eae_a is point mass and uu is the uniform row. For tables T,T′T,T' differing by a transposition of images of PP, expand T2−(T′)2=(T−T′)T+T′(T−T′)T^2-(T')^2=(T-T')T+T'(T-T'). Stochastic contraction in the first term and a convex combination of row differences in the second show that each two-step row's TV changes by at most 8/N8/N. Applying the transposition estimate again,

Pr(d2>60/(N−2)+t)≤2mexp(−Nt2/128). \Pr\!\left(d_2>\sqrt{60/(N-2)}+t\right) \le 2m\exp(-Nt^2/128).

Choose tt proportional to logN/N\sqrt{\log N/N} for the polynomial-tail bound. For large enough NN choose t=1/4t=1/4 to obtain d2<1/2d_2<1/2 with exponentially small exception probability. On this event the maximum TV between two rows of T2T^2 is at most 2d2<12d_2<1. Decomposing a signed zero-sum row into equal positive and negative masses gives TV(pT2,qT2)≤2d2TV(p,q)\mathrm{TV}(pT^2,qT^2)\le 2d_2\,\mathrm{TV}(p,q) for all distributions. Uniform is stationary, so every start converges and d2j≤d2(2d2)j−1d_{2j}\le d_2(2d_2)^{j-1} for j≥1j\ge1. This completes the proof.

Exact mean of two steps with reuse

For N≥4N\ge4,

𝔼P[T(P)2]=U+2N(N−3)(I−U). \mathbb E_P[T(P)^2]=U+\frac{2}{N(N-3)}(I-U).

A table reused across rounds has a small excess two-step return probability. Independent tables in the two rounds give exactly UU in expectation since 𝔼T=U\mathbb E T=U.

To see the correction from reuse, first conjugate PP by LL. The same diagonal/off-diagonal argument shows that 𝔼P[M2]\mathbb E_P[M^2] is a scalar multiple of I−UI-U. To identify the scalar, condition on MM and again average over the independent output relabeling CC. Write rir_i for the rows of MM. In the expansion of tr(MCMC)\operatorname{tr}(MCMC) the terms with equal row indices contribute ∥M∥F2/m\|M\|_F^2/m in expectation. For i≠ji\ne j the assigned columns are a uniform ordered pair of distinct columns, giving expected summand −⟨ri,rj⟩/[m(m−1)]-\langle r_i,r_j\rangle/[m(m-1)] since each row sums to zero. As the columns sum to zero too, ∑i≠j⟨ri,rj⟩=−∥M∥F2\sum_{i\ne j}\langle r_i,r_j\rangle=-\|M\|_F^2. Thus 𝔼Ctr(MCMC)=∥M∥F2/(m−1)\mathbb E_C\operatorname{tr}(MCMC)=\|M\|_F^2/(m-1). Finally divide by tr(I−U)=m−1\operatorname{tr}(I-U)=m-1 and insert the preceding one-step moment. This calculation accounts for the dependence between factors. The TV of the averaged row is distinct from the expected TV of a realized row.

Every two-step entry concentrates

The same model gives a uniform relative error bound for individual transition probabilities. For every fixed K>0K>0, except with probability OK(N−K)O_K(N^{-K}),

maxa,b|(T2)ab−1N−1|=OK((logN)3/2N3/2). \max_{a,b}\left|(T^2)_{ab}-\frac1{N-1}\right| =O_K\!\left(\frac{(\log N)^{3/2}}{N^{3/2}}\right).

In particular T2T^2 is strictly positive with probability tending to one. For a derivation, set s=⌈logN⌉s=\lceil\log N\rceil. Markov's inequality applied to (Kab)s(K_{ab})_s gives Pr(maxKab≥s)≤m2/s!\Pr(\max K_{ab}\ge s)\le m^2/s!, smaller than every fixed negative power of NN asymptotically. Cap all entries of TT at h=2s/Nh=2s/N to obtain BB. Write Fab=(B2)abF_{ab}=(B^2)_{ab}. On the complementary event it equals (T2)ab(T^2)_{ab}, and both random variables lie in [0,1][0,1]. Their means differ by at most m2/s!m^2/s!.

Under a transposition each capped row and column changes by at most 8/N8/N in ℓ1\ell^1, since coordinatewise capping contracts ℓ1\ell^1 distance. In the dot product defining FabF_{ab} the row change costs at most 8h/N8h/N, and the column change costs as much. Hence c=32s/N2c=32s/N^2 works in the transposition estimate. Union bound over m2m^2 cells with tt a sufficiently large KK-dependent multiple of slogN/N3/2s\sqrt{\log N}/N^{3/2}. The exact mean just proved differs from 1/m1/m by at most 2/[N(N−3)]2/[N(N-3)]. Combining the three errors proves the bound.

Fixed-seed numerical check

The rate probe tests the mean matrix and one-step energy by exact integer arithmetic over all tables at N=4,8N=4,8, identifying output translations. It then samples 100 uniform tables at each bit length with seed 20261118. Distances are worst-start distances for each fixed permutation before taking medians across permutations.

Bits Median d1d_1 Median d2d_2 d2≤1/4d_2\le 1/4 Every T2T^2 entry positive
4 0.73333 0.29323 22/100 7/100
5 0.67742 0.19292 97/100 65/100
6 0.66667 0.13063 100/100 99/100
7 0.66142 0.08844 100/100 100/100
8 0.64706 0.05959 100/100 100/100
9 0.63796 0.04032 100/100 100/100

Run from the repository root using the project environment.

OPENBLAS_NUM_THREADS=1 uv run --locked --extra four-bit research/rate_probe.py

The measured Nd2\sqrt N\,d_2 medians are about 0.950.95 at seven bits and 0.910.91 at nine. Whether they approach a positive constant, and whether the worst-start logN\sqrt{\log N} in the bound can be removed, remain open in this analysis.

Literature and provenance

  • The Markov model and convergence question. Lai, Massey and Murphy derive the homogeneous difference chain with independent round keys. O'Connor and Golić, §3 Theorem 5, bound the number of nonzero transitions for a random table. Their Corollary 2 infers typical ergodicity under the explicit additional assumption that the support graph is uniform given its edge count. Their conclusion leaves convergence rates for further work. The proof above works directly with the distribution induced by a permutation, including dependencies between edges. Lai, Massey and Murphy, EUROCRYPT 1991, O'Connor and Golić, ASIACRYPT 1994, pp. 391, 396
  • Differentially 2-uniform permutations. O'Connor's §2.2 explicitly assumes ergodicity in Proposition 2.1 and reports a census of all 8!8! permutations in support of it. All 10,752 three-bit differentially 2-uniform permutations mix. Section 3.1 rigorously proves positivity of the Gram matrix TT⊤TT^\top by row-support intersection, computes the Gram matrix for a three-bit field example and models general off-diagonal intersections by a binomial law. These are direct predecessors for Gram-based rate proofs. The three-round theorem above concerns an unrestricted uniform permutation and uses its true distribution. The paper also reports seven distinct transition matrices in its census. With differences labeled in their original order, the rate probe counts 168 distinct matrices, each arising from 64 permutations, so the distinction matters when comparing counts. O'Connor, EUROCRYPT 1995, pp. 17–21
  • Single-round statistics. O'Connor calculates the exact distribution of XOR-table entries of a uniform permutation. Daemen and Rijmen revisit differential and linear probability distributions, distinguishing random permutations from other distributions over mappings. The zero-probability limit and elementary one-step energy here are consequences of the random-matching count. The dependence of repeated steps enters at T(P)2T(P)^2. O'Connor, On the Distribution of Characteristics in Bijective Mappings, Daemen and Rijmen, Probability Distributions of Correlation and Differentials
  • Walsh and difference spectra. Include the isolated zero difference by taking T̃=1⊕T\widetilde T=1\oplus T. If Wux=N−1/2(−1)u⋅xW_{ux}=N^{-1/2}(-1)^{u\cdot x} and (SP)xy=𝟏y=P(x)(S_P)_{xy}=\mathbf1_{y=P(x)}, then WT̃W=(WSPW)∘2W\widetilde T W=(W S_P W)^{\circ2}, where the square on the right is entrywise. Expanding the left side gives N−2∑x,y(−1)u⋅(x+y)+v⋅(P(x)+P(y))N^{-2}\sum_{x,y}(-1)^{u\cdot(x+y)+v\cdot(P(x)+P(y))}, the square of the corresponding Walsh coefficient. This is the established differential/linear transform. It yields the same spectrum on both sides, including the additional trivial eigenvalue. Canteaut and Roué separately show how affine equivalence can change two-round differential probabilities. Chabaud and Vaudenay, EUROCRYPT 1994, Blondeau, Leander and Nyberg, equation (4), Canteaut and Roué, EUROCRYPT 2015
  • Statistical security under composition. Vaudenay's decorrelation framework develops distribution matrices on tuples and bounds for independently keyed composition. Here the realized one-round key ensembles are independent conditional on PP. Averaging over PP reintroduces dependence, as the exact mean of two steps illustrates. Liu, Tessaro and Vaikuntanathan's Section 4.5 allows a different public permutation per round in its existence argument. Their Appendix A.1 does reuse the patched field inverse. Vaudenay, Decorrelation, Liu, Tessaro and Vaikuntanathan, full paper
  • One public permutation across rounds. Wu, Yu, Cao and Dong and the subsequent general result of Yu, Wu, Yu, Cao and Dong consider key-alternating ciphers that reuse a public random permutation. Their security game limits oracle queries, including access to that permutation. Here the table may be entirely known when selecting the starting pair and evaluating its output law, and there are fresh independent XOR keys. This distinction matters when comparing quantitative conclusions. Wu et al., ASIACRYPT 2020, Yu et al., TCC 2023
  • From pairs to higher orders. Jain et al. prove an Ω(Nlog(1/ϵ))\Omega(N\log(1/\epsilon)) lower bound for approximate four-wise independence in the inverse-walk regime they analyze. Its proximity to pairwise uniformity can coexist with a large obstruction at order four. Jain et al., How Fast Does the Inverse Walk Approximate a Random Permutation?

The patched inverse has an exact two-step distance

Let P(x)=x−1P(x)=x^{-1} on 𝔽N×\mathbb F_N^\times, P(0)=0P(0)=0, and write ψ(x)=(−1)Tr𝔽N/𝔽2(x)\psi(x)=(-1)^{\operatorname{Tr}_{\mathbb F_N/\mathbb F_2}(x)}. Liu, Tessaro and Vaikuntanathan bound the even-bit distance by 5/N5/N for n≥4n\ge4 and report numerical evidence of a constant at most two. They use two inverse applications with a final XOR key, giving the same TV as our third cipher round. Their cases combined with the classical trace/co-trace count yield an exact formula of either parity and the asymptotic constant 7/47/4. These are corollaries of the field calculation and the trace count. Liu, Tessaro and Vaikuntanathan, Appendix A.1, Bojilov, Borissov and Borissov, §5.1

For nonzero a,ba,b the equation P(x)+P(x+a)=bP(x)+P(x+a)=b at x∉{0,a}x\notin\{0,a\} becomes z2+z=(ab)−1z^2+z=(ab)^{-1} with z=x/az=x/a. It has two solutions when the absolute trace on the right is zero and none otherwise. The two exceptional inputs each give b=1/ab=1/a. Hence

NTab=1+ψ((ab)−1)+2𝟏ab=1. NT_{ab}=1+\psi((ab)^{-1})+2\mathbf1_{ab=1}.

Multiply by the same kernel and sum over the intermediate nonzero field element cc. The constant and character terms alone contribute N−1−2+∑c≠0ψ((a−1+b−1)/c)N-1-2+\sum_{c\ne0}\psi((a^{-1}+b^{-1})/c), which is N−4+N𝟏a=bN-4+N\mathbf1_{a=b}. The cross terms with one exceptional input contribute 4+2ψ(b/a)+2ψ(a/b)4+2\psi(b/a)+2\psi(a/b), and the term with two contributes 4𝟏a=b4\mathbf1_{a=b}. For r=b/ar=b/a this gives

N2(T2)ab=N+(N+4)𝟏r=1+2ψ(r)+2ψ(1/r). N^2(T^2)_{ab}=N+(N+4)\mathbf1_{r=1}+2\psi(r)+2\psi(1/r).

For even nn, the diagonal is 2/N+8/N22/N+8/N^2. The printed sum in Case 1 of Liu, Tessaro and Vaikuntanathan's Theorem A.1 substitutes N−2N-2 for the N/2−2N/2-2 ordinary nonzero contributions counted in the preceding sentence. Using their count gives the diagonal above and preserves their stated upper bound. Liu, Tessaro and Vaikuntanathan, p. 43

The diagonal always exceeds the uniform mass. Off the diagonal, only ratios with both traces zero exceed it. Let 𝒦=∑r≠0ψ(r+r−1)\mathcal K=\sum_{r\ne0}\psi(r+r^{-1}). The number of nonzero elements with both traces zero is ∑r≠0(1+ψ(r))(1+ψ(1/r))/4=(N−3+𝒦)/4\sum_{r\ne0}(1+\psi(r))(1+\psi(1/r))/4=(N-3+\mathcal K)/4. Remove r=1r=1 when nn is even and denote the resulting count by AA. Summing the excess mass in a row gives

d2=2N+4+4(−1)nN2−1N−1+A(N+4N2−1N−1). d_2=\frac{2N+4+4(-1)^n}{N^2}-\frac1{N-1} +A\left(\frac{N+4}{N^2}-\frac1{N-1}\right).

The binary Kloosterman estimate |𝒦|≤2N|\mathcal K|\le2\sqrt N gives A=N/4+O(N)A=N/4+O(\sqrt N) and hence d2=7/(4N)+O(N−3/2)d_2=7/(4N)+O(N^{-3/2}). One also gets the finite bound d2≤2/Nd_2\le 2/N for every n≥3n\ge3. Indeed the diagonal excess multiplied by NN is at most 1+7/N1+7/N, the off-diagonal excess multiplied by NN is at most 3/N3/N per positive term, and A≤(N+2N)/4A\le (N+2\sqrt N)/4. Thus Nd2≤7/4+7/N+3/(2N)<2Nd_2\le 7/4+7/N+3/(2\sqrt N)<2 for N≥128N\ge128. For n=3,4,5,6n=3,4,5,6 the exact distances are respectively 3/28,9/80,235/3968,841/322563/28,9/80,235/3968,841/32256. The rate probe verifies the full two-step identity and the resulting distances by independent field arithmetic from two through eight bits. At two bits the exact distance is 2/32/3.
